A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same safety-layer localization and SPPFT study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and renamed experiments and relocated analyses can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V2 reports original layer-wise similarity, localization and fine-tuning experiments on four aligned LLMs, plus attention analyses and layer-transfer results.

after.justification: V4 retains those empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, harmful-data and reverse-DPO experiments, robustness checks and utility evaluations.

M1.justification: Both versions localize contiguous safety layers using final-position vector comparisons, parameter scaling and over-rejection, then freeze those layers during fine-tuning. V4 applies the same freezing principle to additional attack settings; it introduces no new localization or freezing component.

E1.justification: V4 adds instruction-trigger backdoor attacks, harmful-data mixtures, reverse-DPO attacks, Alpaca-clean fine-tuning and AlpacaEval 2.0 evaluation. V2's positive-response 'backdoor' experiment is retained as the implicit attack, so that renaming is not new coverage. The additional scenarios substantially broaden the tested threats and data.

E2.justification: V4 adds evaluated neuron-freezing comparisons based on Wei et al. (2024), labeled NFFT in Table 2, with the frozen parameter proportion matched to SPPFT. It also evaluates Lisa from Huang et al. (2024b) in the harmful-data experiments, Tables 3 and 7. Full fine-tuning and the earlier non-safety-layer freezing controls remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include harmful-mixture sweeps at p=0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 with learning rate 1e-5, matched-proportion neuron-freezing controls, frozen versus standard reverse DPO, and AlpacaEval 2.0 scoring. The original Table 6 hyperparameters and 500-example held-out utility test remain. Section 3.3 also reverses the written angular-gap subtraction.

E4.justification: V4 adds default-template sensitivity checks (Figure 8), Phi-3 localization with alpha=1.2 compared with the retained alpha=0.8 result (Table 5), harmful-mixture sensitivity, and additional attention cases (Figures 9–12). The non-safety-layer and transfer analyses are retained. Appendix A.4.5 describes partial contiguous safety-layer freezing, replacing v2's qualitative account of noncontiguous freezing.

E5.justification: Both retain 500 random query-pair repetitions, shaded variability in similarity plots, and the standard-deviation discussion for scaling-factor selection. V4 does not introduce fine-tuning seed counts, confidence intervals or formal significance tests; its additional result tables use the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V4 adds substantial result blocks for NFFT, explicit-trigger backdoors, harmful data, AlpacaEval and reverse DPO. Existing values also change: Llama-2 normal-data Rouge-L for SPPFT/FullFT changes from 0.254/0.248 in v2 Table 3 to 0.248/0.270 in v4 Table 2, reversing their ranking without explaining the revision. Initial-model utility entries are omitted, while the main localization table and transfer scores are retained.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the angular-gap definition from angle(N,N) minus angle(N,M) to angle(N,M) minus angle(N,N), correcting its sign relative to the plotted positive gaps. The residual-layer equation and underlying mathematical framework remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims about contiguous safety layers, their localization and SPPFT remain. V4 broadens the abstract and introduction's defense framing from non-malicious normal/positive-response data to fine-tuning attacks generally, while narrowing the conclusion's mechanistic novelty claim from parameter-level to layer-wise analysis.

C2.justification: New Appendix A.4.1 distinguishes benign local fine-tuning from an API threat model with content filtering and no attacker access to weights. Appendix A.5.4 adds neuron-concentration and distributional explanations of the observed layer behavior. Conversely, v2's explicit qualification that layers beyond the identified safety range may still affect security is removed.

D1.justification: V4 newly specifies 4,000 implicit examples, 1,000 normal examples, the 1,500-plus-1,500 backdoor composition, and settings for harmful-data experiments and Lisa. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified sample counts. V2 Table 2's instruction to exclude the positive-response prefix when computing utility scores is no longer stated.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning through Appendix A.2's taxonomy of alignment-stage, fine-tuning-stage and post-fine-tuning defenses. It acknowledges Wei et al.'s security-neuron analysis and explicitly distinguishes its safety layers from Zhao et al.'s concurrent layer-editing work. This replaces v2's much broader assertion of missing parameter-level analyses and defenses.

P1.justification: The introduction and central methodological explanations are extensively rewritten, including regrouping the cosine analysis into pairing rules followed by a common calculation. Section 4 consolidates previously separate experimental subsections, moves the ablation discussion into the appendix, and reorganizes the appendices around related work, localization, defense and discussion.

P2.justification: V4 redesigns and consolidates the main results into Table 2 with scenario blocks and NFFT columns, relocates the earlier non-safety-layer table to Appendix Table 8, and adds several tables and Figures 8–12. Existing main figures receive label, legend and axis refinements. Tables 3 and 7 display the same new harmful-data results in different layouts.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses important validation gaps through matched neuron-freezing and Lisa comparisons, broader attack tests, and prompt/scaling robustness checks. The explicit deployment assumptions and expanded prior-work discussion also improve interpretability and positioning. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including unexplained utility-score revisions and Table 10's out-of-range harmfulness score of 22.30. Broad security-preservation language remains insufficiently qualified: Table 3 reports SPPFT harmful rates of 68.3% and 78.8% at p=0.2.
